title: Matter and Its Three States
seo_title: Grade 5 Science: Matter and Its Three States Worksheets (MATATAG)
standard_text: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space; it exists as solids, liquids and gases with different properties; matter is made of particles; matter changes state when heated or cooled. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 5, Quarter 1: Materials)
meta_desc: Free Grade 5 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 1: Materials): states of matter, particles in matter, changes of state, properties of materials and matter investigations. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Matter has mass and takes up space.
key_sub: Solids keep their shape, liquids take the shape of their container, and gases fill it.
body_html:
How to think about it

All matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving.

  • Solid: particles packed tightly, fixed shape. Liquid: particles slide past each other. Gas: particles far apart and fast.
  • Heating makes particles move faster: melting, evaporation, sublimation. Cooling: freezing, condensation, deposition.
  • Properties like hardness, flexibility, conductivity and magnetism decide what a material is used for.
Example

Water vapor forms drops on a cold window. What change is this?

gas → liquid

Answer: condensation

Example

When ice melts, does its mass change?

the particles are the same

Answer: no

Common mistakes

  • Thinking air is not matter.
  • Mixing up evaporation and condensation.
  • Thinking mass changes when something melts.

faq.q: What are the three states of matter?
faq.a: Solid, liquid and gas. They differ in how closely packed the particles are and how they move.
A solid turning straight into a gas, like mothballs (naphthalene) slowly getting smaller in a cabinet.
Air has mass and takes up space, so it is matter even though we cannot see it.

items.q: What is it called when a gas turns into a liquid?
items.e: Water drops form on a cold glass.

items.q: Which states of matter cannot be squashed into a smaller space?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: Is liquid soap a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: It has a definite volume but no definite shape.

items.q: Which of these is a liquid?
items.e: A liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape.

items.q: Which of these is a solid?
items.e: A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume.

items.q: Is air a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: Air is a gas.

items.q: Which state of matter keeps its own shape?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: What is it called when a solid turns directly into a gas?
items.e: Dry ice sublimes.

items.q: Which state of matter takes the shape of its container but keeps its volume?
items.e: Liquids flow.

items.q: Which property can you measure with a balance?
items.e: A balance compares masses.

items.q: Is oxygen a solid, a liquid or a gas?

items.q: Is the bubbles in a fizzy drink a solid, a liquid or a gas?

items.q: Which state of matter keeps the same volume but changes shape?

items.q: Which state of matter spreads out to fill any container?

items.q: Which of these does not dissolve in water?
items.e: Cornstarch does not dissolve. You can still see it in the water, or it settles to the bottom.

items.q: Which of these does not dissolve in water?
items.e: Small pebbles does not dissolve. You can still see it in the water, or it settles to the bottom.

items.q: Vincent drops a sugar cube into warm tea and waits. Which property is he testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's solubility.

items.q: Which of these does not dissolve in water?
items.e: Sand does not dissolve. You can still see it in the water, or it settles to the bottom.

items.q: Which object will a magnet pick up?
items.e: A steel screw contains iron, so it is attracted to a magnet. Many metals, like aluminum, copper and gold, are not.

items.q: Diane tries to scratch a mineral with a steel nail. Which property is she testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's hardness.

items.q: Rafael drops a stone into a graduated cylinder of water. Which property is he testing?

items.q: What happens to the particles in water when it boils?
c: They move faster and spread far apart.
items.e: Heating gives particles more energy.

items.q: Which metal object will not stick to a magnet?
items.e: A brass key is a metal, but it has no iron in it, so a magnet does not attract it. Iron and steel are attracted to magnets.

items.q: Which of these dissolves in water?
items.e: Salt dissolves: it breaks into particles too small to see and spreads through the water.

items.q: Lance puts a rod in hot water and feels how fast the other end warms up. Which property is he testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's thermal conductivity.

items.q: A bulb is in a circuit with a gap. Which object placed across the gap will make the bulb light?

items.q: Which object is an electrical insulator?
items.e: A rubber eraser does not let electricity flow through it. All the other objects are metals, which are conductors.

items.q: A sponge gets smaller when squeezed. Does this mean solids can be squashed?
c: No. The air in the holes is squeezed out; the solid itself does not shrink.
Yes, all solids can be squashed.
items.e: Think about what is in the holes.

items.q: A flat beach ball has a mass of 411 g. After it is pumped full of air, its mass is 422 g. What is the mass of the air inside?
items.e: 422 − 411 = 11 g. The air added mass, so air is matter.

items.q: Sheila's mystery liquid freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C. Which liquid is it most likely?
items.e: Pure water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C. The temperatures where a substance changes state help identify it.

items.q: Gabriel tests 4 objects in a circuit. The bulb lights for a key, a foil ball and a coin, but not for a button. Which conclusion is best?
c: Only the button is a conductor.
The key, foil and coin are conductors; the button is an insulator.
items.e: Objects that let the bulb light are conductors. The button stops the electricity, so it is an insulator.

items.q: Trisha finds a shiny gray rock that is attracted to a magnet. Which mineral could it be?
items.e: Magnetite contains a lot of iron, so it is attracted to a magnet. Quartz, talc and calcite are not.

items.e: Comparing the mass before and after adding air shows that the air itself has mass.

items.q: A flat beach ball has a mass of 519 g. After it is pumped full of air, its mass is 532 g. What is the mass of the air inside?
items.e: 532 − 519 = 13 g. The air added mass, so air is matter.

items.q: Learners test which material keeps ice frozen longest: foil, wool or plastic wrap. The ice in wool lasts longest. What does this show?
c: Wool is the best conductor of heat.
Wool is the best thermal insulator of the three.
items.e: Wool slows the movement of heat from the air to the ice, so the ice melts more slowly.

items.q: A flat basketball ball has a mass of 467 g. After it is pumped full of air, its mass is 485 g. What is the mass of the air inside?
items.e: 485 − 467 = 18 g. The air added mass, so air is matter.

items.q: Emmanuel notices that a bicycle tire looks a little flat on a cold morning and fuller on a hot afternoon. No air was added. Why?
c: The tire made more air during the day.
Warm air particles move faster and push harder on the tire.
items.e: The same air is inside. When it warms, the particles move faster and push outward more.

items.q: A flat ball has a mass of 499 g. After it is pumped full of air, its mass is 513 g. What is the mass of the air inside?
items.e: 513 − 499 = 14 g. The air added mass, so air is matter.
